title: Thinking recursively
description: Recognize the pattern. Build the solution. Make it faster.

parts.title: Your starting point
parts.label: Pre-test
parts.description: A short, unassisted check of what you already know. This is a baseline, not a lesson grade.
parts.question: Complete the four diagnostic questions without assistance.

parts.title: A smaller version of the same problem
parts.label: Discover
parts.description: Open the nesting dolls, watch the calls build up, then follow the returns back out.
parts.question: Explain base cases, recursive reduction, and pending calls or stack unwinding, using the nesting dolls and worked Fibonacci example.
parts.theory: Recursion solves a problem using smaller instances of the same problem. A base case is handled directly without another recursive call. A recursive case reduces the input and uses the smaller result. Calls wait on a stack until their subproblems return. In the Russian nesting doll analogy, opening a doll reveals a smaller similar doll; the smallest solid doll is the base case. Then results return outward, one waiting call at a time. Use this analogy conversationally and ask one brief check-in question at a time.

parts.title: Choose, build, and trace
parts.label: Build & trace
parts.description: Use the worked Fibonacci example to design a naive Climbing Stairs solution, then construct and trace your own call tree.
parts.question: Build a naive climb_stairs(4) call tree, explain suitability and recurrence, identify stack depth, and run your own recursive Python code.
parts.theory: For the standard direct base cases n=0 and n=1, climb_stairs(4) returns 5, has 9 calls, reaches four stack frames, and calls state 2 twice. Use only short hints, never final answers or completed code.

parts.title: Remember the work you have already done
parts.label: Optimize
parts.description: Study a worked Fibonacci cache example, locate redundancy in your own stairs tree, then memoize your own stairs code.
parts.question: Study the worked Fibonacci cache example, count repeated calls in the naive climb_stairs(4) tree, memoize your own code, and identify the main change.
parts.theory: For naive stairs(4), state 2 occurs twice and one occurrence repeats work. Dictionary lookup before branching and storage before return avoids recomputation. Memoization uses O(n) time, cache, and stack space under unit-cost arithmetic and dictionary lookup.

parts.title: A new problem, on your own
parts.label: Transfer
parts.description: Apply recursion and memoization to Grid Unique Paths with the same question-specific hints.
parts.question: Explain base conditions, reduction, and pending calls using multiple choice. Construct a naive unique_paths(2,2) tree before coding. Run correctness tests, then memoize a copy of your own code. Empty grids have zero paths and a single-cell grid has one path.
parts.theory: Paths(r,c)=Paths(r-1,c)+Paths(r,c-1). Empty dimensions return zero; a 1x1 grid returns one. A direct one-axis base case is also valid. With that shortcut the 2x2 tree has no duplicate states; larger test inputs demonstrate overlapping subproblems. Memoization uses O(rows*cols) time/cache and O(rows+cols) stack space under unit-cost arithmetic. Give hints only, never complete answers.

parts.title: Reflect on your experience
parts.label: Reflect
parts.description: A few final questions after the timed lesson.
parts.question: Rate the hints and describe your experience and understanding of recursion.

stairs-suitability.prompt: Why is recursion suitable for Climbing Stairs? Identify smaller instances of the same problem.

stairs-recurrence.prompt: State your recurrence and base cases.

memo-example-explanation.prompt: Explain how the lookup and storage order avoids repeating a Fibonacci branch.

intro-reduction.prompt: How does the Fibonacci example reduce the problem toward a base case?

options.label: It calls the function with n-1 and n-2 until reaching small inputs
It increases n on each call

intro-stack.prompt: What happens to a pending call while its smaller calls execute?

options.label: It forgets its input as soon as a child starts
It retains its input and unfinished work, then resumes when a child returns
Every node in the entire tree stays on the stack at once

stairs-depth.prompt: For climb_stairs(4), returning directly for n=0 and n=1, what is the maximum number of simultaneous stack frames? Count the root as one.

stairs-two-count.prompt: In the full naive climb_stairs(4) tree, returning directly for n=0 and n=1, how many calls have input 2?

stairs-extra-count.prompt: How many of those input-2 calls repeat work after the first computation?

stairs-main-change.prompt: What is the main change from the naive function to the memoized function?

options.label: Memoization changes which stair sequences are counted
Memoization removes the need for base cases
Memoization stores and reuses results for identical inputs instead of recomputing them
Memoization guarantees no extra memory is used

grid-base.prompt: Which base conditions correctly describe this grid problem?

options.label: An empty grid has 0 paths and a single-cell grid has 1 path
An empty grid has 1 path and a single-cell grid has 0 paths
The function needs no base conditions

grid-reduction.prompt: Which pair of smaller states can be combined to solve unique_paths(rows, cols)?

grid-stack.prompt: What does a pending grid call keep while a smaller call executes?

options.label: Only the final answer, already known
No state, because its frame is removed immediately
Its current dimensions and unfinished work combining smaller results
A frame for every grid cell simultaneously
